Title: Workplace learning through peer groups in medical school clerkships.

Journal/Date: Medical education online (2014)

MeSH Keywords: Clinical Clerkship, Education, Medical, Undergraduate, Humans, Learning, Peer Group, Qualitative Research, Surveys and Questionnaires, Workplace


--- ABSTRACT ---
[PURPOSE]: When medical students move from the classroom into clinical practice environments, their roles and learning challenges shift dramatically from a formal curricular approach to a workplace learning model. Continuity among peers during clinical clerkships may play an important role in this different mode of learning. We explored students' perceptions about how they achieved workplace learning in the context of intentionally formed or ad hoc peer groups.
[METHOD]: We invited students in clerkship program models with continuity (CMCs) and in traditional block clerkships (BCs) to complete a survey about peer relationships with open-ended questions based on a workplace learning framework, including themes of workplace-based relationships, the nature of work practices, and selection of tasks and activities. We conducted qualitative content analysis to characterize students' experiences.
[RESULTS]: In both BCs and CMCs, peer groups provided rich resources, including anticipatory guidance about clinical expectations of students, best practices in interacting with patients and supervisors, helpful advice in transitioning between rotations, and information about implicit rules of clerkships. Students also used each other as benchmarks for gauging strengths and deficits in their own knowledge and skills.
[CONCLUSIONS]: Students achieve many aspects of workplace learning in clerkships through formal or informal workplace-based peer groups. In these groups, peers provide accessible, real-time, and relevant resources to help each other navigate transitions, clarify roles and tasks, manage interpersonal challenges, and decrease isolation. Medical schools can support effective workplace learning for medical students by incorporating continuity with peers in the main clinical clerkship year.

[METHOD]: Seventy-one students from three Veterans Affairs-based clerkship rotations at the University of California, San Francisco, School of Medicine participated in a peer-to-peer handoff session from 2008 to 2011. The authors transcribed student comments from four handoff sessions and used qualitative content analysis to identify and compare advice across clerkships.
[RESULTS]: Students shared advice about workplace culture, content learning, logistics, and work-life balance. Common themes included expectations of the rotation, workplace norms, specific tasks, learning opportunities, and learning strategies. Comments about patient care and work-life balance were rare. Students emphasized different themes for each clerkship; for example, for some clerkships, students commented heavily on tasks and content learning, while in another students focused on workplace culture and exam preparation.
[CONCLUSIONS]: These findings characterize the transitions that third-year students undergo as they rotate into new clinical training environments. Students emphasized different aspects of each clerkship in the advice they passed to their peers, and their comments often describe informal norms or opportunities that official clerkship orientations may not address. Peer-to-peer handoffs may help ease transitions between clerkships with dissimilar cultures and expectations.

Title: How medical students co-regulate their learning in clinical clerkships: a social network study.

Journal/Date: BMC medical education (2022)

MeSH Keywords: Clinical Clerkship, Education, Medical, Undergraduate, Humans, Learning, Social Networking, Students, Medical


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: Self-regulated learning is a key competence to engage in lifelong learning. Research increasingly acknowledges that medical students in clerkships need others to regulate their learning. The concept of "co-regulated learning" captures this act of regulating one's learning by interacting with others. To effectively cultivate such skills in students, we need to increase our understanding of co-regulated learning. This study aimed to identify the purposes for which students in different phases of clinical training engage others in their networks to regulate their learning.
[METHODS]: In this social network study, we administered a questionnaire to 403 medical students during clinical clerkships (65.5% response rate). The questionnaire probed into the composition of students' co-regulatory networks and the purpose for which they engaged others in specified self-regulated learning activities. We calculated the proportion of students that engaged others in their networks for each regulatory activity. Additionally, we conducted ANOVAs to examine whether first-, second-, and third-year students differed in how they used their networks to support self-regulation.
[RESULTS]: Students used others within their co-regulatory networks to support a range of self-regulated learning activities. Whom students engaged, and the purpose of engagement, seemed to shift as students progressed through clinical training. Over time, the proportion of students engaging workplace supervisors to discuss learning goals, learning strategies, self-reflections and self-evaluations increased, whereas the proportion of students engaging peers to discuss learning strategies and how to work on learning goals in the workplace decreased. Of all purposes for which students engaged others measured, discussing self-reflections and self-evaluations were consistently among the ones most frequently mentioned.
[CONCLUSIONS]: Results reinforce the notion that medical students' regulation of learning is grounded in social interactions within co-regulatory networks students construct during clerkships. Findings elucidate the extent to which students enact self-regulatory learning within their co-regulatory networks and how their co-regulatory learning behaviors develop over time. Explicating the relevance of interactions within co-regulatory networks might help students and supervisors to purposefully engage in meaningful co-regulatory interactions. Additionally, co-regulatory interactions may assist students in regulating their learning in clinical workplaces as well as in honing their self-regulated learning skills.

[INTRODUCTION]: Peer-assisted learning (PAL) is widely used in undergraduate medical education, and collaborative learning is gaining momentum. Unfortunately, literature shows that students utilise their peers less during undergraduate clerkships, a phase when PAL is known to be particularly useful to students and their clinical-reasoning learning process. key_findings.finding: Direct evidence supports that workplace learning through peer groups does occur during medical-school clerkships. In a qualitative survey study comparing continuity-model clerkships with traditional block clerkships (54 respondents), students described peers as real-time resources for clinical expectations, patient/supervisor interactions, rotation transitions, implicit rules, and benchmarking knowledge and skills; authors concluded that formal and informal workplace peer groups supported many aspects of workplace learning. Limitations include self-reported perceptions, qualitative content analysis, modest response/sample size, and no objective learning outcomes.

Peer learning is manifested in authentic clinical-workplace activity, not only scheduled instruction. A 2025 focused ethnography used 20 interviews with students/residents/supervisors plus 31.5 hours of observation of 26 undergraduate students across internal medicine, neurology, surgery, ophthalmology, and emergency departments. Students used multiple forms of peer-assisted learning to advance clinical reasoning, but processes were often implicit, facilitation inconsistent, and individualistic/competitive tendencies could inhibit participation.

source_tools.relevance: Direct observational and interview evidence across clinical workplaces

key_findings.finding: A 2025 design-based study provides intervention evidence that workplace peer learning can be deliberately enabled. Across four stakeholder work conferences (101 participants), a 2-month paired-consultation pilot involving 41 students was judged successful; students reported that observing peers supported clinical-reasoning learning, while supervisors became more enthusiastic. Proposed mechanisms were reciprocal vulnerability, psychological safety, shared responsibility, autonomy/flexibility, supervisor support, and a learner community within a community of practice. Evidence is preliminary and largely evaluative/self-reported, without a controlled comparison or demonstrated patient/assessment outcomes.

A social-network study of 403 students in clinical clerkships found that students' co-regulatory networks supported learning goals, strategies, reflection, and self-evaluation. Peer use for discussing learning strategies and working on goals decreased across clinical-training years as engagement with workplace supervisors increased, indicating that peer learning is present but its role changes with experience and is not necessarily the dominant source of regulation later in training.

source_tools.relevance: Large empirical clerkship study of peer co-regulation

key_findings.finding: Peer-to-peer handoffs directly transmitted workplace knowledge across clerkship transitions. In a qualitative study of 71 students across three VA-based rotations, students shared rotation-specific norms, expectations, tasks, learning opportunities, logistics, and strategies; patient-care discussion was rare. This is strong evidence for peer transmission of tacit workplace/navigation knowledge, but the intervention was a handoff session rather than naturally observed learning, and outcomes beyond perceived transition support were not measured.

source_tools.relevance: Direct evidence of peer transmission of clinical-workplace norms

key_findings.finding: Other qualitative studies reinforce mechanisms without directly testing attainment. Eighteen students in focus groups described clinical reasoning as contextually and socially mediated and called for greater peer and patient learning; nine longitudinally followed students reported that peer relationships and discussions helped meaning-making and professional-identity formation in clinical workplaces. These studies are interpretive, small, and self-report based, so they support plausibility/mechanisms rather than causal effectiveness.

source_tools.relevance: Student perspective on workplace clinical reasoning

key_findings.finding: The 2013 BEME review of 53 longitudinal community/hospital placement studies identified continuity of peer group, alongside continuity of patients, supervision, mentorship, and location, as a predominant mechanism associated with successful longitudinal placements. However, most evaluations were student opinions or assessment results, and the review did not isolate peer-learning effects; therefore it is supportive contextual evidence rather than direct proof of peer-group causation.

Classroom or scheduled near-peer instruction should not be conflated with workplace learning. The Manchester interpretative phenomenological study involved eight participants in a near-peer clinical-skills scheme and found safety, egalitarianism, camaraderie, and social congruence as mechanisms; participants contrasted these sessions with senior-led clinical teaching. It is relevant to mechanisms of peer instruction, but because the evidence concerns PAL sessions rather than peer learning embedded in patient-care work, it is indirect for the workplace-learning question.

source_tools.relevance: Near-peer instructional study; useful contrast but not direct workplace evidence

entities.name: Clerkship peer workplace learning
observations: Question concerns whether medical students learn through peer groups during clinical clerkships.

entities.name: Clerkship peer learning exists
observations: In a qualitative survey of 54 clerkship students, formal and informal peer groups supported clinical expectations, patient and supervisor interactions, rotation transitions, implicit rules, and benchmarking of knowledge and skills.
Evidence is self-reported and qualitative, with no objective learning outcomes.

entities.name: Peer learning in clinical work
observations: A focused ethnography across five clinical departments observed peer-assisted learning used during authentic clinical activity to advance clinical reasoning.
Peer learning was often implicit; inconsistent facilitation and competitive or individualistic cultures could inhibit participation.

entities.name: Paired consultation pilot
observations: A two-month paired-consultation pilot with 41 students was judged successful and linked peer observation with clinical-reasoning learning.
Proposed mechanisms included psychological safety, reciprocal vulnerability, shared responsibility, autonomy, flexibility, supervisor support, and learner community.

entities.name: Peer workplace knowledge transfer
observations: Peer-to-peer handoffs across three clerkship rotations transmitted norms, expectations, tasks, logistics, learning opportunities, and strategies.
Patient-care discussion was rare and outcomes beyond perceived transition support were not measured.

entities.name: Clerkship co-regulation networks
observations: A social-network study of 403 clinical-training students found peers involved in learning goals, strategies, reflection, and self-evaluation.
Peer use declined across training years as supervisor engagement increased, suggesting a changing rather than absent peer role.

entities.name: Longitudinal peer continuity
observations: A review of 53 longitudinal community and hospital placement studies identified continuity of peer groups as a recurring mechanism associated with successful longitudinal placements.
The review did not isolate peer-learning effects and relied substantially on opinions or assessment results.
